claims.source: This comparison shows that the site size changes approximately ∼1.7-fold (43 nts to 70 nts) over this range whereas the length of the SSB-ssDNA molecules changes approximately ∼13-fold (from ∼6.5 μm to ∼0.5 μm).
claims.evidence: This is determined by comparing the data from Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: The extent of condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA exceeds what can be explained by simple changes in binding mode or site size.
claims.source: We note that the apparent site size of SSB can vary depending on the ssDNA used owing to exclusion of SSB from regions capable of forming stable secondary structure (Lohman and Overman, 1985); however, the reported change in site size for natural M13 ssDNA is only ∼2.2-fold (from 35 to 77) over a comparable range (1 mM to 300 mM NaCl), which is insufficient to account for our observations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the observed 13-fold change in length to the expected 1.7-2.2-fold change based on site size.

claims.claim: Mg(OAc)2 induces a large condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA nucleoprotein fibers that plateaus between 1 and 2 mM.
claims.source: Mg(OAc)2 induces a large condensation of nucleoprotein fibers that plateaus between 1 and 2 mM, and results in complexes that are as short as those produced with the much higher monovalent salt concentrations (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Escherichia coli maintains its intracellular osmolality by adjusting the intracellular concentration of glutamate, which ranges from ∼30 to 260 mM when cells are grown in media containing from ∼100 to 1100 mM solute.
claims.source: Escherichia coli maintains its intracellular osmolality by adjusting the intracellular concentration of glutamate, which ranges from ∼30 to 260 mM when cells are grown in media containing from ∼100 to 1100 mM solute (Richey et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: At low concentrations of NaGlu (below 100 mM), the condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA was dominated by the presence of 1 mM Mg(OAc)2.
claims.source: At low concentrations of NaGlu (i.e. below 100 mM), the condensation was dominated by the presence of 1 mM Mg(OAc)2; however, the observed condensation became dominated by NaGlu at higher concentrations (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The shorter, more condensed SSB-coated ssDNA molecules likely represent the physiologically relevant condensation state of the SSB-ssDNA complex as estimated by the in vivo concentration and composition of salts.
claims.source: Extrapolating from this data, the shorter, more condensed molecules that we observe likely represent the physiologically relevant condensation state of the SSB-ssDNA complex as estimated by the in vivo concentration and composition of salts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on salt-dependent condensation.

claims.claim: Force-extension curves of ssDNA alone at salt concentrations greater than 25 mM NaOAc demonstrate hysteresis due to the formation of secondary structure in the ssDNA.
claims.source: The force-extension curves for ssDNA alone at salt concentrations greater than 25 mM NaOAc demonstrate hysteresis (i.e. the force-extension curves obtained by increasing and decreasing force do not overlap) due to the formation of secondary structure in the ssDNA (Bosco et al., 2014) see also, (Zhang et al., 2001; Saleh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4C and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Hysteresis was absent in the force-extension curves measured in the presence of SSB, except at 750 mM NaOAc.
claims.source: Interestingly, this hysteresis was absent in the force-extension curves measured in the presence of SSB (Figure 4D), except at 750 mM NaOAc, the highest salt concentration that we used in our magnetic tweezer experiments.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The modest hysteresis at 750 mM NaOAc is consistent with partial dissociation of SSB at high concentrations of NaOAc.
claims.source: This modest hysteresis at the highest concentration of NaOAc is consistent with our interpretation that the decrease in the amplitude of the fluorescence enhancement measured during equilibrium titrations with SSBf is due to partial dissociation of SSB at concentrations of NaOAc greater than 750 mM (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the hysteresis data with the fluorescence data.

claims.claim: The absence of hysteresis in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the structures are always at equilibrium, and that there are no kinetically trapped intermediates.
claims.source: More importantly, the absence of hysteresis in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the structures are always at equilibrium, and that there are no kinetically trapped intermediates, neither short range nor the more likely long range random interactions (Schaper et al., 1991), that would contribute to non-equilibrium behavior.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of no hysteresis.

claims.claim: The intramolecular condensation observed is intrinsic to a reversible equilibrium folding of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
claims.source: We therefore infer that the intramolecular condensation that we observe is intrinsic to a reversible equilibrium folding of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of hysteresis in the force-extension curves.

claims.claim: The extent of salt-induced condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA is dependent on the force applied.
claims.source: As the concentration of NaOAc increases, the length of the SSB-coated ssDNA monotonically decreases, or condenses, (Figure 4E); however, the extent of the condensation is dependent on the force applied.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The shear force applied by flow during TIRF microscopy is approximately between 0.1 and 0.5 pN.
claims.source: Since the salt-induced condensation of the molecules measured in the TIRF experiments (Figure 4E, black squares) is most similar to the relative condensation observed in the magnetic tweezer experiments that were performed at forces between 0.1 and 0.5 pN (Figure 4E, orange and gray circles), we estimate that this is approximately the shear force applied by flow during TIRF microscopy within our microfluidic cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the TIRF and magnetic tweezer data.

claims.claim: The salt-induced condensation observed with SSBf-ssDNA complex is in qualitative agreement with the data obtained with wild-type SSB.
claims.source: Importantly, because the salt-induced condensation of the SSBf-ssDNA complex is in qualitative agreement with the data obtained with wild-type SSB, we conclude that the salt-induced condensation observed in Figure 3 and Figure 4D,E is dominated by intramolecular bridging in cis, mediated by oligomers of SSB, rather than any property of the modified SSBf (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the SSBf and wild-type SSB data.

claims.claim: The addition of SSB resulted in an additional 3100 (±550) kBT at salt concentrations from 25 to 250 mM NaOAc relative to relaxing ssDNA.
claims.source: The addition of SSB resulted in an additional 3100 (±550) kBT (represented as ΔΔE) at salt concentrations from 25 to 250 mM NaOAc relative to relaxing ssDNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, open red circles, dashed line).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Only at 750 mM NaOAc was there a substantial reduction in the ΔΔE, consistent with SSB dissociation at these high salt concentrations.
claims.source: Only at the highest salt concentration that we measured, 750 mM NaOAc, did we measure a substantial reduction in the ΔΔE, consistent with our interpretation that SSB dissociates at these high salt concentrations, but not measurably below 250 mM NaOAc.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The total energy contribution of SSB binding is nearly constant (i.e. isoenergetic) within error, with respect to increasing salt concentrations (up to ∼250 mM NaOAc).
claims.source: While the total energy contribution of SSB binding is nearly constant (i.e. isoenergetic) within error, with respect to increasing salt concentrations (up to ∼250 mM NaOAc), the contribution of each individual SSB tetramer should (and does) vary due to the transition in the site size across the range of salt conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the energy calculations shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The energy of SSB binding to ssDNA corresponds to ∼11 (±2) kBT per SSB tetramer.
claims.source: Accounting for the change in site size as the concentration of salt increases, the energy of SSB binding to ssDNA in our measurement corresponds to ∼11 (±2) kBT per SSB tetramer (assuming ∼200–320 SSB tetramers per ssDNA molecule), which is in reasonable agreement with the binding energy previously reported (Zhou et al., 2011; Suksombat et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data and compared to previous work.

claims.claim: When RecO was added in a stoichiometric ratio to SSB, the nucleoprotein fiber shortened ∼10% relative to SSB-alone across the entire force spectrum, and hysteresis was not evident.
claims.source: When RecO was added in a stoichiometric ratio to SSB, the nucleoprotein fiber shortened ∼10% relative to SSB-alone across the entire force spectrum, and hysteresis was not evident (purple lines, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The absence of hysteresis in the presence of RecO suggests that RecO functions primarily in trans to promote annealing of complimentary strands, but not in cis to permit formation of non-specific secondary structures.
claims.source: The absence of hysteresis in the presence of RecO is interesting because RecO is known to facilitate annealing of complementary ssDNA in the presence of SSB (Kantake et al., 2002), suggesting that RecO functions primarily in trans to promote annealing of complimentary strands, but not in cis to permit formation of non-specific secondary structures.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of no hysteresis with RecO and its known function.

claims.claim: When RecR was added in the presence of both SSB and RecO, severe hysteresis was observed in the force-extension curves.
claims.source: When we added RecR in the presence of both SSB and RecO, we observed severe hysteresis in the force-extension curves (Figure 5B, compare solid and dashed green lines).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The hysteresis observed with RecOR suggests that RecR bridges distant contacts, either through protein–protein interactions or by facilitating intramolecular annealing in cis of regions of micro-homology.
claims.source: This hysteresis suggests that RecR bridges distant contacts, either through protein–protein interactions or by facilitating intramolecular annealing in cis of regions of micro-homology, and that these contacts are disrupted as the fiber is stretched by the magnetic tweezers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of hysteresis with RecOR.

claims.claim: The energy contribution from RecOR-mediated bridging was ∼2000 kBT (or ∼10 kBT per SSB tetramer).
claims.source: The energy contribution from RecOR-mediated bridging was ∼2000 kBT (or ∼10 kBT per SSB tetramer).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The energy contribution from RecOR-mediated bridging is essentially the same as the energetic contribution from SSB binding to ssDNA alone.
claims.source: Interestingly, this energy contribution is essentially the same as the energetic contribution from SSB binding to ssDNA alone (∼9–13 kBT per tetramer, see previous section), indicating that RecOR bridges distant SSB tetramers and those tetramers must be disrupted as the molecule is stretched by increasing force.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the energy contributions of RecOR and SSB.

claims.claim: RecOR forms a complex that binds to SSB-bound to ssDNA, and in doing so, both modulates the wrapped-state, or binding-mode, of SSB to induce macroscopic changes and serves as a scaffold to bridge distant sites along the SSB-ssDNA nucleoprotein fiber.
claims.source: We conclude that when incubated together, RecOR forms a complex that binds to SSB-bound to ssDNA, and in doing so, both modulates the wrapped-state, or binding-mode, of SSB in order to induce macroscopic changes and serves as a scaffold to bridge distant sites along the SSB-ssDNA nucleoprotein fiber.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on RecOR effects.

claims.claim: The macroscopic condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA could occur either through the association of stable octamers or through ssDNA by the direct binding of distant sites to a single tetramer.
claims.source: This macroscopic condensation could occur either through the association of stable octamers or through ssDNA by the direct binding of distant sites to a single tetramer.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the molecular mechanism of condensation.

claims.claim: The extent of condensation is greatest under conditions where ssDNA is fully wrapped around the protein in the SSB65 binding mode, making octamer formation more likely.
claims.source: The extent of condensation, however, is greatest under conditions where ssDNA is fully wrapped around the protein in the SSB65 binding mode, making the former possibility more likely.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on salt-dependent condensation.

claims.claim: The addition of SSB eliminated the salt-induced hysteresis caused by formation of DNA secondary structure through intramolecular annealing in cis.
claims.source: In our force-spectroscopy experiments, the addition of SSB (or SSB and RecO) eliminated the salt-induced hysteresis caused by formation of DNA secondary structure through intramolecular annealing in cis.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The change in energy due to SSB binding (when summed over a single molecule of ssDNA) is nearly isoenergetic across a large salt concentration range.
claims.source: When we compare the energetic contribution of SSB binding to ssDNA, relative to the salt-induced effects on the ssDNA polymer energetics (excluding the contributions from long range secondary structure by comparing the 'relaxing' ssDNA force-extension curves), the change in energy due to SSB binding (when summed over a single molecule of ssDNA) is nearly isoenergetic across a large salt concentration range (Figure 5A, compare the slope for SSB, red-filled circles, to relaxing ssDNA alone, open black circles, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the energy calculations shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The isoenergetic landscape implies a homeostasis with regard to the energetics of SSB, relative to ssDNA, at physiological salt concentrations, making the absolute intracellular salt concentration nearly unimportant relative to other cellular processes working on or with the SSB-ssDNA complex.
claims.source: This is both interesting and unexpected as it implies a homeostasis with regard to the energetics of SSB, relative to ssDNA, at physiological salt concentrations, making the absolute intracellular salt concentration nearly unimportant relative to other cellular processes working on or with the SSB-ssDNA complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the isoenergetic nature of SSB binding across salt concentrations.

claims.claim: The relatively constant energy contribution of SSB across the ssDNA is made possible by a net change in the microscopic binding modes of SSB such that all (or most) ssDNA is effectively coated by SSB, albeit with each SSB tetramer engaged in a different number of nucleotides and a different number of SSB tetramers engaged at each salt concentration.
claims.source: We propose that this relatively constant energy contribution across the ssDNA is made possible by a net change in the microscopic binding modes of SSB in such a way that all (or most) ssDNA is effectively coated by SSB, albeit with each SSB tetramer engaged in a different number of nucleotides and a different number of SSB tetramers engaged at each salt concentration.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the isoenergetic landscape.

claims.claim: Previous AFM imaging of SSB bound to M13mp7 ssDNA measured contour lengths of ∼920 nm in the low salt, 35-nucleotide binding mode, and 560 nm in the high salt, 65-nucleotide binding mode, representing a 1.6-fold increase upon going from high to low salt.
claims.source: Previous AFM imaging of SSB bound to M13mp7 ssDNA (7249 nts) measured contour lengths of SSB-ssDNA of ∼920 nm in the low salt, 35-nucleotide binding mode, and 560 nm in the high salt, 65-nucleotide binding mode; this change represents a 1.6-fold increase upon going from high to low salt, or a decrease of 60% upon going from low to high salt (Hamon et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The observed approximately 13-fold compaction of SSB-coated ssDNA from 6.5 μm in the absence of salt to 0.5 μm at 750 mM NaOAc exceeds the expected twofold change based on site size alone.
claims.source: Since denatured λ-phage DNA is 6.6-fold longer than M13mp7 ssDNA, we expected our SSB-ssDNA would be approximately 6.1 μm long in low salt and compacted by 1.6-fold to approximately 3.7 μm long in high salt (up to ∼300 mM Na+); however, we observed an approximately fourfold compaction over this range. A substantially greater degree of compaction of the complexes was measured upon further increase in salt concentration – from 6.5 μm in the absence of salt to 0.5 μm at 750 mM NaOAc – which is a 13-fold compaction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the observed data to expected values based on previous work.

claims.claim: If the site size was the dominant factor determining the condensation state of SSB-coated ssDNA, then the maximum change in length should be approximately twofold.
claims.source: If the site size was the dominant factor determining the condensation state of SSB-coated ssDNA, then the maximum change in length should be approximately twofold, yet we measure a ∼13-fold decrease in length.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the observed data to expected values.

claims.claim: SSB exhibits limited cooperativity between tetramers at higher salt concentrations, where it also forms octamers which might serve as an intramolecular bridges between distant sites along the ssDNA resulting in condensation.
claims.source: We propose that an explanation derives from the fact that SSB does not simply bind to ssDNA as an array of globular units, but instead exhibits limited cooperativity between tetramers, at higher salt concentrations, where it also forms octamers (Lohman and Bujalowski, 1988; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1989a, b) which might serve as an intramolecular bridges between distant sites along the ssDNA resulting in the condensation that we observe (Chrysogelos and Griffith, 1982; Griffith et al., 1984; Hamon et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The population of the various SSB-binding modes depends not only on intracellular solution conditions, but also on the SSB concentration itself due to the established effects of 'competition' between DNA-binding modes with different site sizes, affinities, and cooperativities.
claims.source: Although the molecular nature of the condensing species is unknown, we also note that the population of the various SSB-binding modes depends not only on intracellular solution conditions, but also on the SSB concentration itself due to the established effects of 'competition' between DNA-binding modes with different site sizes, affinities, and cooperativities (Schwarz and Stankowski, 1979; Bujalowski et al., 1988); therefore, with SSB in excess over ssDNA – which is the cellular situation – multiple modes coexist and may serve to keep the amounts of bound SSB nearly constant.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The high degree of salt-induced compaction of SSB-ssDNA observed is in good qualitative agreement with early ultracentrifugation experiments performed with SSB-saturated M13-phage ssDNA.
claims.source: Finally, although the high degree of salt-induced compaction of SSB-ssDNA that we observed was surprising based on previous AFM and EM studies, our results are in good qualitative agreement with early, largely unexplained, ultracentrifugation experiments performed with SSB-saturated M13-phage ssDNA (Schaper et al., 1991): our changes in length with salt concentration map exactly on the reported changes in sedimentation coefficients for the SSB-M13 ssDNA complexes.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The force-extension measurements of unlabeled, wild-type SSB recapitulates the relative condensation of SSBf-coated ssDNA observed in the direct visualization experiments.
claims.source: Importantly, the force-extension measurements of unlabeled, wild-type SSB recapitulates the relative condensation of SSBf-coated ssDNA observed in the direct visualization experiments, indicating that the observed condensation of the fluorescently modified nucleoprotein complex in Figure 1C and Figure 3C–G is not a consequence of using modified SSB, SSBAF488, or SSBf, but rather is due to an intrinsic, salt-induced conformational change resulting in intramolecular re-organization along the nucleoprotein fiber.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the wild-type SSB and SSBf data.

claims.claim: The absence of hysteresis in force-extension curves in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the intramolecular condensation is not due to the formation of distant ssDNA–ssDNA contacts, but rather is driven by the microscopic reorganization of SSB along the ssDNA.
claims.source: The absence of hysteresis in our force-extension curves in the presence of SSB is strong evidence that the intramolecular condensation that we observe is not due to the formation of distant ssDNA–ssDNA contacts, but rather is driven by the microscopic reorganization of SSB along the ssDNA, which in turn contributes to a macroscopic folding of the molecule.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of no hysteresis.

claims.claim: Dimerization of SSB tetramers (i.e. octamer formation) is a well-established phenomenon at increasing but still physiologically relevant intracellular salt concentrations.
claims.source: First, dimerization of SSB tetramers (i.e. octamer formation) is a well-established phenomenon at increasing but still physiologically relevant intracellular salt concentrations (Chrysogelos and Griffith, 1982; Bujalowski and Lohman, 1987), which can linearly vary from 0.23 to 0.93 molal K+ ion and from 0.03 to 0.26 molal glutamate ion in response to changes in the osmolality of the growth medium (Richey et al., 1987) see also, (Epstein and Schultz, 1965) (Epstein and Schultz, 1966).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: SSB exhibits long-range, intersegmental transfer, which likely proceeds through direct, tetramer transfer within a ternary intermediate comprising SSB and two ssDNA molecules without proceeding through a free-protein intermediate.
claims.source: Second, SSB exhibits long-range, intersegmental transfer (Lee et al., 2014), the latter of which likely proceeds through direct, tetramer transfer within a ternary intermediate comprising SSB and two ssDNA molecules without proceeding through a free-protein intermediate (Kozlov and Lohman, 2002a, b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The intramolecular condensation observed provides evidence that the sum of transient SSB interactions across the SSB-ssDNA fiber might explain how many SSB tetramers can simultaneously engage in distant ssDNA sites to contribute to an intramolecular, folded polymer that is highly dynamic and 'fluid'.
claims.source: This phenomenon has primarily been described as a transient intermediate during rapid, stopped flow kinetics; however, we believe that the intramolecular condensation that we observe here provides evidence that the sum of these transient interactions across the SSB-ssDNA fiber might explain how many SSB tetramers can simultaneously engage in distant ssDNA sites to contribute to an intramolecular, folded polymer that is highly dynamic and 'fluid', undergoing constant, steady–steady state protein turnover and diffusion at equilibrium.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on condensation and previous knowledge of SSB dynamics.

claims.claim: The rapid exchange of SSB protein and the absence of net protein loss under steady-state conditions, but rapid dissociation in the absence of free protein during salt-jump experiments, corroborates the dynamic nature of the SSB-ssDNA complex.
claims.source: This is corroborated by the rapid exchange of SSB protein (Figure 1F) and the absence of net protein loss under steady-state conditions (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the rapid dissociation in the absence of free protein during salt-jump experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as well as the ability of SSB labeled with different fluorophores to exchange and form mixed complexes (JCB, unpublished observations), a phenomenon also demonstrated for eukaryotic RPA (Gibb et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the manuscript and citations to other work.

claims.claim: SSB-ssDNA is macroscopically organized and regulated through microscopic interactions, similar to the most basic organization of eukaryotic chromatin.
claims.source: Similar to nucleosomes, SSB binds and wraps a DNA polymer around itself (albeit ssDNA instead of dsDNA), interacts with dozens of proteins via a short acidic peptide tail, and exhibits complex cooperative and anti-cooperative behavior that is modulated by salt concentration. Our observation that SSB-ssDNA is macroscopically organized and regulated through microscopic interactions is surprisingly similar to the most basic organization of eukaryotic chromatin and highlights the important role of SSB, not simply as a kinetic trap for ssDNA, but as an organizational and regulatory scaffold during DNA metabolism (Shereda et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison to chromatin organization.

claims.claim: The organizational and regulatory role of SSB is likely controlled by the acidic, intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail of SSB, which is required for cooperative binding of SSB to ssDNA.
claims.source: This organizational and regulatory role is likely controlled by the acidic, intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail of SSB, which is required for cooperative binding of SSB to ssDNA (Kozlov et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: A cadre of proteins including the χ subunit of DNA polymerase III, PriA, PriB, RecG, RNaseHI, Exonuclease I, and RecO bind to the C-terminal tail of SSB and either remodel the SSB-ssDNA complex or regulate enzymatic ssDNA metabolism.
claims.source: Recent studies have identified a cadre of proteins, including the χ subunit of DNA polymerase III, PriA, PriB, RecG, RNaseHI, Exonuclease I, and RecO, that bind to the C-terminal tail of SSB and either remodel the SSB-ssDNA complex or regulate enzymatic ssDNA metabolism (Cadman and McGlynn, 2004; Shereda et al., 2007, 2008; Lu and Keck, 2008; Kozlov et al., 2010a, 2010b, 2015; Wessel et al., 2013; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014; Petzold et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: These many proteins may regulate access to ssDNA by binding to SSB and altering either compaction/de-compaction most likely by perturbing the microscopic binding state of SSB.
claims.source: Extrapolating from our observations in this work, these many proteins may regulate access to ssDNA by binding to SSB and altering either compaction/de-compaction most likely by perturbing the microscopic binding state of SSB.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on RecOR and extrapolated to other SSB-binding proteins.

claims.claim: RecO binds directly to SSB in the absence and presence of RecR.
claims.source: Indeed, we demonstrate that this condensation occurs not only with increasing osmolality, but also by the addition of RecO, which binds directly to SSB, in the absence and presence of RecR (Ryzhikov et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work and the experimental data in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Altering the macromolecular state of SSB-ssDNA by bridging distant sites could reduce the three-dimensional space required to facilitate homology-dependent annealing of ssDNA.
claims.source: In the case of RecO and RecOR, altering this macromolecular state by bridging distant sites could reduce the three-dimensional space required to facilitate homology-dependent annealing of ssDNA (Berg et al., 1981; Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012), which occurs by a second order kinetic process (Berg et al., 1981; Kantake et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2006; Bell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: RecO has been shown to slow the rate of one-dimensional diffusion, or sliding, of SSB on ssDNA.
claims.source: Similarly, RecO has been shown to slow the rate of one-dimensional diffusion, or sliding, of SSB on ssDNA (Zhou et al., 2011), which is consistent with the small energy contribution of RecO and RecOR binding we observe here, where RecO contributes an additional ∼1–2 kBT per SSB tetramer.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work and is consistent with the experimental data.

claims.claim: By slowing the rate of diffusion of SSB on ssDNA, RecO might facilitate both annealing and RecA nucleation by increasing the lifetime of transiently exposed ssDNA.
claims.source: By slowing the rate of diffusion of SSB on ssDNA, RecO might facilitate both annealing and RecA nucleation by increasing the lifetime of transiently exposed ssDNA.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which RecO facilitates annealing and RecA nucleation.

claims.claim: The long range interactions induced by RecR could be due to phasing of SSB via its interaction with RecO, creating microscopic gaps on the ssDNA that allow distant sites with micro-homology to anneal, forming intramolecular secondary structure.
claims.source: The long range interactions induced by RecR could also be due to phasing of SSB via its interaction with RecO, creating microscopic gaps on the ssDNA that allow distant sites with micro-homology to anneal, forming intramolecular secondary structure (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which RecR induces long-range interactions.

claims.claim: Microscopic gaps created by RecOR could facilitate the nucleation of RecA filaments during homologous recombination by exposing short segments of ssDNA between SSB tetramers.
claims.source: In its biological context, these microscopic gaps could also facilitate the nucleation of RecA filaments during homologous recombination by exposing short segments of ssDNA between SSB tetramers, either by inducing a conformational change that physically disrupts the SSB-ssDNA complex to create gaps or by increasing the lifetime of transiently exposed ssDNA created during SSB sliding along the ssDNA (Bell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the biological function of RecOR-induced gaps, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: SSBAF488 maintains a high, albeit attenuated, affinity for ssDNA.
claims.source: This protein maintains a high, albeit attenuated, affinity for ssDNA (Bell, 2011; Bell et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: SSBf is particularly suitable as an ensemble ssDNA-biosensor due to the large, linear increase in fluorescence upon ssDNA binding.
claims.source: SSBAF488 is particularly suitable for single molecule measurements due to its relative photostability, whereas an alternative biosensor derived from fluorescein-5-maleimide, SSBf, is particularly suitable as an ensemble ssDNA-biosensor due to the large, linear increase in fluorescence upon ssDNA binding (Dillingham et al., 2008; Bell, 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The energy contribution of RecO to the SSB-ssDNA energy was modest, accounting for ∼250 kBT (or ∼1.2 kBT per SSB tetramer).
claims.source: The energy contribution of RecO to the SSB-ssDNA energy was modest, accounting for ∼250 kBT (or ∼1.2 kBT per SSB tetramer).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The addition of RecR contributed a modest amount of energy when the SSB-RecO-ssDNA complex was relaxing (an additional ∼220 kBT or ∼1 kBT per SSB tetramer).
claims.source: The addition of RecR––so that SSB, RecO, and RecR were all present––again, contributed a modest amount of energy when the complex was relaxing (an additional ∼220 kBT or ∼1 kBT per SSB tetramer)
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the force-extension data shown in Figure 5C.

results.result: SSB-coated ssDNA molecules undergo reversible salt-induced condensation in the presence of free SSB, with fluorescence intensity remaining constant during condensation, indicating protein redistribution rather than dissociation. In the absence of free SSB, condensation is still reversible but accompanied by partial protein dissociation (20% at 100 mM, 60% at 400 mM NaOAc).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35 provide direct experimental evidence from TIRF microscopy showing reversible condensation with and without free protein. The fluorescence intensity data (C29) supports redistribution over dissociation in steady-state conditions, while the reversibility experiments (C32-C35) demonstrate both the dynamic nature and quantify protein loss in the absence of free SSB. The displacement experiment (C30-C31) validates the fluorescence-based measurements.

results.result: The observed 13-fold condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA (from 6.5 μm to 0.5 μm) exceeds the expected ~2-fold change based on SSB site size transitions (43 to 70 nucleotides), indicating that simple binding mode changes cannot account for the observed condensation. This contradicts expectations from previous AFM studies showing only 1.6-fold changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 and C70-C72 provide converging evidence from ensemble titrations and single-molecule measurements. The site size measurements (C36) are consistent with known SSB binding modes, but the length measurements (C39) demonstrate a discrepancy that cannot be explained by site size alone (C40, C72). The comparison to previous AFM work (C70-C71) strengthens the conclusion that a novel condensation mechanism is at play.

results.result: Mg(OAc)2 induces condensation of SSB-coated ssDNA that plateaus at 1-2 mM, producing complexes as short as those formed at much higher monovalent salt concentrations. Under physiologically relevant conditions (considering E. coli intracellular glutamate concentrations), the condensed state likely represents the physiological conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C41 and C43 provide direct experimental evidence for Mg2+-induced condensation. Claim C42 establishes the physiological context through citation to previous work on E. coli osmolality regulation. Claim C44 is a reasonable inference connecting the experimental observations to physiological relevance, though it remains somewhat speculative without direct in vivo validation.

results.result: SSB eliminates hysteresis in force-extension curves of ssDNA (except at 750 mM NaOAc), indicating that SSB-coated ssDNA is always at equilibrium without kinetically trapped intermediates. This demonstrates that the observed condensation is due to reversible equilibrium folding driven by SSB reorganization rather than secondary structure formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 provide direct experimental evidence from magnetic tweezers showing absence of hysteresis with SSB. The exception at 750 mM (C46-C47) is consistent with partial SSB dissociation observed in other experiments. Claims C66 and C77 provide the mechanistic interpretation that is well-supported by the hysteresis data. The logic connecting absence of hysteresis to equilibrium behavior and ruling out secondary structure is sound.

results.result: The extent of salt-induced condensation is force-dependent, with TIRF microscopy measurements corresponding to forces of 0.1-0.5 pN. Wild-type SSB recapitulates the condensation behavior observed with fluorescently labeled SSB variants, confirming that condensation is intrinsic to SSB-ssDNA and not an artifact of fluorescent labeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 provide direct measurements and reasonable inference about shear forces in TIRF. Claims C52 and C76 are critical controls demonstrating that the fluorescent modifications do not cause the observed condensation. The qualitative agreement between SSBf and wild-type SSB across different experimental approaches strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: SSB binding to ssDNA exhibits an isoenergetic landscape across physiological salt concentrations (25-250 mM NaOAc), with total energy contribution remaining constant at ~3100 kBT (~11 kBT per tetramer). This implies homeostasis in SSB-ssDNA energetics, making absolute intracellular salt concentration relatively unimportant for SSB function.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 provide quantitative energy measurements from force spectroscopy that are internally consistent and agree with previous work (C56). Claims C67-C68 present the isoenergetic interpretation, which is well-supported by the data. Claim C69 proposes a mechanism involving microscopic binding mode changes, which is reasonable speculation based on the data but remains unproven. The biological interpretation (C68) is a significant inference that requires further validation.

results.result: RecO binding to SSB-coated ssDNA causes ~10% condensation across all forces and contributes ~250 kBT (~1.2 kBT per SSB tetramer) without introducing hysteresis. The absence of hysteresis suggests RecO functions primarily in trans to promote annealing rather than in cis to permit secondary structure formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C94 provide direct experimental measurements of RecO effects. Claim C58 presents a mechanistic interpretation based on the absence of hysteresis and known RecO function. The inference is logical but somewhat speculative, as the trans vs. cis distinction is not directly demonstrated. The energy contribution is modest but measurable and consistent across experiments.

results.result: RecOR (RecO + RecR) induces severe hysteresis in force-extension curves, contributing ~2000 kBT (~10 kBT per SSB tetramer) from bridging interactions. This energy is equivalent to SSB binding energy itself, indicating RecOR bridges distant SSB tetramers and modulates SSB binding mode while serving as a scaffold for long-range interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C61, and C95 provide direct experimental measurements. Claims C60, C62, and C63 present mechanistic interpretations that are well-supported by the data. The equivalence of RecOR bridging energy to SSB binding energy (C62) is a significant finding. The conclusion that RecOR both modulates binding mode and bridges distant sites (C63) is supported by the combination of condensation and hysteresis observations.

results.result: The macroscopic condensation likely occurs through SSB octamer formation (dimers of tetramers) rather than single tetramers binding distant sites, as condensation is greatest under SSB65 binding mode conditions. This is supported by established octamer formation at physiological salt concentrations and SSB's ability to undergo intersegmental transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 present speculation about mechanism with C65 providing some supporting inference from the data. Claims C73, C78-C79 cite established SSB properties that support the octamer hypothesis. Claim C80 is highly speculative about the dynamic nature of the condensed state. While the octamer mechanism is plausible and supported by prior literature, the current data do not definitively distinguish between octamer-mediated bridging and other mechanisms. Direct structural or biochemical evidence for octamers in the condensed state is lacking.

results.result: The observed SSB-ssDNA condensation is consistent with early ultracentrifugation data and suggests SSB functions as an organizational scaffold similar to chromatin, with regulation likely controlled by the C-terminal tail and its many interacting proteins that may modulate compaction/decompaction states.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 provides supporting evidence from prior work. Claims C82-C83 present an interesting analogy to chromatin that is supported by the data but remains somewhat speculative. Claims C84-C85 extrapolate from the RecOR findings to other SSB-binding proteins, which is reasonable speculation but lacks direct experimental support. The organizational scaffold model is compelling but requires additional validation with other SSB-interacting proteins.

results.result: RecO/RecOR may facilitate homology-dependent annealing and RecA nucleation by bridging distant sites to reduce search space, slowing SSB diffusion to increase ssDNA exposure lifetime, and creating microscopic gaps through SSB phasing that expose ssDNA segments for RecA binding or allow micro-homology annealing.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by citations and current data. Claim C87 presents a reasonable inference about functional consequences. Claim C88 is supported by prior work. Claims C89-C91 are largely speculative mechanisms that, while consistent with the data and biologically plausible, lack direct experimental validation in this study. These represent testable hypotheses for future work rather than established findings.

results.result: Background on SSB: SSB is essential for DNA maintenance, binds ssDNA with variable footprints (30-70 nt) reflecting different binding modes, protects ssDNA, and exhibits salt-dependent cooperativity. Previous EM and AFM studies showed ~2-fold length changes corresponding to binding mode transitions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C15 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims set the context for the current work and are well-established in the literature. The prior structural studies (C12-C14) are particularly important as they establish the baseline expectations that the current work exceeds.

results.result: Background on SSB-interacting proteins: Multiple proteins interact with SSB's C-terminal tail to modulate SSB-ssDNA complexes. RecO catalyzes annealing and promotes RecA-dependent recombination with RecR and RecF. RecR enhances RecO's affinity for SSB but neither displaces SSB. RecOR must act through conformational changes in SSB-ssDNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C27 provide essential background on RecO/RecR function supported by appropriate citations. Claim C27 presents a logical inference from the lack of direct RecA-SSB/RecO/RecR interactions that is well-supported by prior work. This background establishes the rationale for studying RecOR effects on SSB-ssDNA condensation.

results.result: Methodological note: SSBAF488 maintains high affinity for ssDNA and is suitable for single-molecule imaging, while SSBf is suitable for ensemble measurements due to large fluorescence enhancement upon binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 describe the properties of the fluorescent SSB variants used in the study, supported by citations to prior characterization work. These are important methodological details that justify the use of these reagents.

results.result: Summary of main findings: SSB-coated ssDNA exhibits intramolecular condensation exceeding expectations from binding mode transitions. SSB engages in long-range reversible interactions under high-salt conditions. RecO and RecOR further condense the complex, with RecOR functioning to alter long-range interactions by modulating wrapping and bridging distant sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 summarize the main findings that are supported by the detailed experimental results in other claim groups. These represent the key conclusions of the paper and are well-supported by the totality of the evidence presented.
